title: National macro-surveillance of overweight and obesity in India, Bangladesh, and Nepal: A systematic review of global versus Asian BMI thresholds and associated factors
content:
by Rameshwor Parajuli, Wilna Oldewage-Theron, Surya Raj Niraula

Introduction

Evaluating how global versus Asian-specific body mass index (BMI) thresholds impact macro-level population surveillance is essential for addressing South Asia’s changing epidemiological landscape. We systematically synthesized the prevalence of overweight and obesity and identified significant associated factors across India, Bangladesh, and Nepal to compare the diagnostic impact of these distinct BMI criteria.

Materials and methods

Following PRISMA guidelines, we searched electronic databases including PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ), Google Scholar, and Index Medicus for the South-East Asia Region (IMSEAR) for peer-reviewed studies published between 2015 and 2026 utilizing nationally representative datasets from 2011 onward. Overlapping surveys were grouped into cohort families to prevent duplicate counting. Studies were stratified by BMI criteria and demographic subgroups.

Results

Shifting from global (≥25 kg/m2) to Asian-specific (≥23 kg/m2) BMI cutoffs triggered a substantial prevalence jump in reported overweight and obesity outcomes. Between 2011 and 2022, overweight and obesity prevalence among reproductive-aged Bangladeshi women more than doubled, reaching 55.3% under the Asian-specific threshold. Significant associated factors mapping revealed a dominant wealth-urbanization cluster (higher household wealth, higher education, and urban residency) and significant obstetric factors (higher parity and cesarean delivery) across all three nations. Crucially, direct dietary intake and physical activity metrics were virtually unmeasured, trapping regional literature in an asset-association loop.

Conclusions

Relying on global BMI criteria severely masks the South Asian overnutrition crisis and delays vital public health interventions. National health agencies must integrate localized, Asian-specific BMI cutoffs into regional reporting frameworks and shift surveillance focus from simple demographic asset proxies toward direct, validated dietary and behavioral metrics.
author: Rameshwor Parajuli
